source_refs.note: 'P-value and its Importance' under topic 7.3, as printed (PDF 97, printed 93).

blocks.text: The p-value shows the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis. It measures the probability of getting the observed results, or more extreme results, if the null hypothesis is true. A small p-value supports the rejection of the null hypothesis because it suggests that the result is unlikely to have occurred by chance. The p-value is compared with the significance level, such as (0.05), to make a decision.

For example, suppose a teacher wants to test whether a new teaching method improves students' marks. The null hypothesis states that the new method has no effect. After analysing the test scores, the p-value is found to be (0.03). Since (0.03 < 0.05), the null hypothesis may be rejected. This means there is statistical evidence that the new teaching method may have improved students' performance.

Similarly, in medicine, researchers may test whether a new drug is more effective than an old drug. If the p-value is (0.01), it gives strong evidence that the improvement is unlikely to be due to chance alone.

P-values help simplify statistical decisions and support data-driven conclusions. A clear understanding of p-values helps avoid mistakes, such as rejecting or accepting a hypothesis without proper evidence.
